title: Probability
outcomes: Describe random experiments, sample spaces and events — simple, compound, mutually exclusive, exhaustive, equally likely and complementary.
Compute probabilities by the classical, statistical (relative frequency) and axiomatic approaches, and convert between odds and probability.
Apply the addition theorems, conditional probability, the compound (multiplication) theorem and the test of independence.
Build the probability distribution of a discrete random variable and find its expected value and variance, using the properties of expectation.

meta.exam_tip: Probability carries several MCQs every attempt. The classic marks: dice (36 cases), cards (52), coins (2ⁿ), "at least one" = 1 − P(none), P(A or B) formula, conditional probability and E(X). Write the sample space size first — that alone removes most errors.

concepts.title: Random experiments, sample space and events
body: A random experiment can be repeated under the same conditions; all its outcomes are known in advance but the actual outcome cannot be predicted (tossing a coin, drawing a card). The set of all outcomes is the sample space S; each outcome is a sample point. An event is any subset of S.
Simple (elementary) event: a single outcome. Compound (composite) event: made of two or more outcomes — "an even number on a die".

Mutually exclusive (incompatible) events: no two can occur together (head and tail on one toss); P(A and B) = 0. Exhaustive events: together they cover every possible outcome; P(A or B or …) = 1. Equally likely (equi-probable) events: no reason to expect one more than another.
Complementary event A′ (or Ā): "A does not occur". A and A′ are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so P(A′) = 1 − P(A).
Counting reminders: n coins → 2ⁿ outcomes; two dice → 36; a pack → 52 cards (4 suits × 13; 26 red, 26 black; 12 face cards; 4 aces); selections use ⁿCᵣ.
concepts.analogy: The sample space is the full menu; an event is your order — one dish (simple) or a combo (compound).
concepts.work: Risk registers list possible outcomes (events) of a project; making sure the list is exhaustive and the categories mutually exclusive is the same discipline.

concepts.title: Definitions of probability and odds
body: Classical (a priori) definition — Bernoulli and Laplace: if an experiment has n mutually exclusive, exhaustive and equally likely outcomes and m are favourable to A, P(A) = m/n. Limitations: needs equally likely outcomes; fails when the number of outcomes is infinite; limited to coins, dice, cards and similar cases where no prior knowledge is required.
Statistical (empirical / relative frequency) definition: if A occurs f times in n trials, P(A) = limit of f/n as n becomes very large — provided the limit exists and is finite.

Set-theoretic form: P(A) = n(A)/n(S) for equally likely sample points. Axiomatic (modern) definition: P is a function on events with (i) P(A) ≥ 0, (ii) P(S) = 1, (iii) for mutually exclusive events, P(A₁ or A₂ or …) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + …. Consequences: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, P(∅) = 0, P(A′) = 1 − P(A).
Odds in favour of A = m : (n − m) (favourable : unfavourable). Odds against A = (n − m) : m. If odds in favour are a : b, P(A) = a/(a + b).
concepts.analogy: Classical probability reads the rule book of the game; statistical probability watches the game played thousands of times.
concepts.work: Insurance premiums rest on the relative-frequency definition — claim rates from past data. Credit-rating default probabilities are also empirical.

concepts.title: Mutually exclusive vs independent
body: Mutually exclusive: A and B cannot happen together — P(A and B) = 0.

Independent: the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other — P(B|A) = P(B), equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). This product rule is the necessary and sufficient condition. For three events, all pairwise products and the triple product must hold.
If A and B are independent, so are (A, B′), (A′, B) and (A′, B′). Two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.
concepts.analogy: Mutually exclusive: two people who cannot sit on the same chair. Independent: two people in different cities flipping coins.
concepts.work: Auditors relying on two controls assume they fail independently — if both depend on the same IT system, they are not independent and the combined assurance is overstated.

concepts.title: Addition theorems
body: Theorem 1 (mutually exclusive): P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Theorem 2: for k mutually exclusive events, add all k probabilities.
Theorem 3 (any two events): P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). It is the general rule — use it unless you are sure the events are mutually exclusive.

Theorem 4 (three events): P(at least one of A, B, C) = S₁ − S₂ + S₃, where S₁ is the sum of the three single probabilities, S₂ the sum of the three pairwise joint probabilities [P(A and B) + P(B and C) + P(C and A)], and S₃ = P(all three together).
Useful forms: P(A only) = P(A) − P(A and B); P(neither) = 1 − P(A or B); expected frequency = N × probability.
concepts.analogy: Counting people who like tea or coffee: add both lists, then remove those you counted twice.
concepts.work: If 30% of invoices lack a PO and 20% lack approval, and 8% lack both, then 42% have at least one control gap — the addition theorem in audit sampling.

concepts.title: Conditional probability and compound probability
body: Conditional probability of B given A: P(B|A) = P(A and B)/P(A), P(A) > 0. It revises probability using the information that A has happened (e.g. drawing without replacement changes the composition).
Compound (multiplication) theorem: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A) = P(B) × P(A|B). For three events: P(A, B, C together) = P(A) P(B|A) P(C|A and B).
For independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B); P(A, B, C together) = P(A) P(B) P(C).
"At least one" of independent events: 1 − P(A′) P(B′) P(C′).
concepts.analogy: Conditional probability is weather forecasting after seeing dark clouds — the clouds (A) change the chance of rain (B).
concepts.work: Probability that a customer pays on time given he paid late last quarter is a conditional probability that credit teams use for collection priorities.

concepts.title: Random variable and probability distribution
body: A random (stochastic) variable assigns a real number to every sample point (number of heads in three tosses). Discrete: takes isolated values (heads, accidents, defects). Continuous: takes any value in an interval (height, weight).

Probability distribution of a discrete X: the list of values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ, where every pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1 (probability mass function). For a continuous X, a density function f(x) ≥ 0 with total area 1 gives probabilities over intervals.
concepts.analogy: A frequency distribution describes what happened; a probability distribution describes what is expected to happen.
concepts.work: Demand forecasts for inventory are often a probability distribution of daily demand rather than one number.

concepts.title: Expected value and variance
body: Expected value (mathematical expectation, mean): E(X) = μ = Σpᵢxᵢ. E(X²) = Σpᵢxᵢ²; for any function, E[g(X)] = Σpᵢ g(xᵢ).
Variance: V(X) = σ² = E(X − μ)² = E(X²) − [E(X)]²; SD = √V(X).
Properties: E(k) = k; E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y); E(kX) = kE(X); E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) if X and Y are independent. For y = a + bX: E(y) = a + bE(X), V(y) = b²V(X), SD(y) = |b| SD(X).
concepts.analogy: Expected value is the long-run average pay-out per play if a game is repeated many times.
concepts.work: Expected credit loss, expected warranty cost and expected value of a contingent liability are all Σ probability × amount.

solution.title: (a) 36 outcomes
solution.text: Sum 8: first die 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 with the second die making up 8 — five cases → 5/36. Sum ≥ 10: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 cases → 1/6. Doublets: 6 → 1/6.

illustrations.title: Addition theorem and a test of independence
illustrations.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.2. Find P(A or B), P(A|B), P(neither) and P(A only). Are A and B independent?

solution.text: P(A) × P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 = P(A and B), so A and B are independent (equivalently, P(A|B) = P(A) = 0.5). They are not mutually exclusive, since P(A and B) ≠ 0.

illustrations.title: "At least one", "exactly one" and drawing without replacement
illustrations.q: (a) Three reviewers independently spot a particular error with probabilities 0.6, 0.5 and 0.4. Find P(at least one spots it), P(all three) and P(exactly one). (b) A box has 3 defective and 5 good parts. Two are drawn one after another. P(both defective) without and with replacement?

solution.title: (b)
solution.text: Without replacement: 3/8 × 2/7 = 3/28 (conditional probability — the second draw depends on the first). With replacement: 3/8 × 3/8 = 9/64 (independent draws).

illustrations.title: Expected value and variance of a distribution
illustrations.q: (a) Orders per hour X at a help desk: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 with probabilities 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1. Find E(X), V(X), and the mean and variance of Y = 3X − 4. (b) A player pays ₹250 to draw one ball from a bag of 1 white and 3 red balls; he gets ₹500 for white and ₹200 for red. Expected net gain?

checks.label: expected gain of the game (net of fee)

jobs.title: How much assurance do two controls give?
jobs.situation: A payment is released only after a system check (fails to catch an error 10% of the time) and a manager review (misses 20% of errors). Management claims a 98% catch rate.
steps: If the two controls work independently, P(both miss) = 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.02, so P(at least one catches) = 0.98.
Test independence: the manager reviews only payments the system has passed, using the same vendor master. If the vendor master is wrong, both miss together.
Where controls share a common cause, P(both miss) > 0.02 and the 98% claim is overstated.
Report the dependency and recommend an independent check of vendor-master changes.
jobs.takeaway: Multiplying failure probabilities is valid only for independent controls.

checks.label: P(at least one control catches the error)

jobs.title: Expected value for a provision decision
jobs.situation: A customer dispute: legal counsel estimates 50% chance of paying ₹0, 30% of paying ₹8 lakh and 20% of paying ₹20 lakh.
steps: Check the probabilities sum to 1 (a valid distribution).
Accounting standards may require the most likely outcome or the expected value depending on the situation — the statistics give the input, the standard decides the measure.
jobs.takeaway: Expected value = Σ probability × amount; it is the long-run average, not the amount that will actually be paid.

viva.q: State the classical definition of probability and its limitations.
viva.model: When an experiment can end in n equally likely, mutually exclusive and exhaustive ways, and m of those ways favour the event A, the probability of A is m divided by n. Its limitations are that it needs equally likely outcomes, it cannot be used when the total number of outcomes is infinite, and it applies only to simple situations like coins, dice and cards where no prior knowledge is needed.

viva.q: What is the difference between mutually exclusive events and independent events?
viva.model: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together; the occurrence of one rules out the other, so the probability of A and B together is zero. Independent events can occur together, and the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other, so the probability of A and B is P of A times P of B. Two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.

viva.q: What is the expected value of a random variable, and what are its main properties?
viva.model: The expected value, or mathematical expectation, is the sum of each value of the random variable multiplied by its probability: E of X equals sigma p x. Properties: the expectation of a constant is the constant; the expectation of a sum is the sum of the expectations; E of a plus b X equals a plus b times E of X; and for independent variables the expectation of the product is the product of the expectations. The variance is E of X squared minus the square of E of X.

viva.q: What do odds in favour and odds against an event mean? If the odds in favour are 3 to 5, what is the probability?
viva.model: Odds in favour of an event are the ratio of favourable cases to unfavourable cases, and odds against are the ratio of unfavourable cases to favourable cases. If the odds in favour are 3 to 5, there are 3 favourable out of 8 cases, so the probability is 3 by 8, or 0.375.

cases.title: Default risk in a small loan book
cases.case: A cooperative bank has 1,000 personal loans of ₹5,00,000 each. 60% of borrowers are salaried and 40% self-employed. Past data show that 2% of salaried borrowers and 5% of self-employed borrowers default. A borrower is chosen at random from the book. Assume that a defaulted loan is fully lost.

mcqs.q: What is the probability that the borrower is salaried and defaults?
mcqs.explain: Multiplication theorem: P(S and D) = P(S) × P(D|S) = 0.6 × 0.02 = 0.012.

mcqs.q: What is the probability that the borrower defaults?
mcqs.explain: Default happens either with a salaried or with a self-employed borrower (mutually exclusive): 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. 0.07 simply adds the two rates; 0.05 is the self-employed rate alone.

mcqs.q: What are the odds against a randomly chosen borrower defaulting?
What is the expected loss on the whole book?
mcqs.explain: Expected number of defaults = 1,000 × 0.032 = 32; expected loss = 32 × ₹5,00,000 = ₹1.6 crore.
